title: Episode 34: GitHub Actions and Workflows
description: Workflow YAML structure, CI/CD, automation, and the Actions marketplace.
concepts: What GitHub Actions are: event-driven automation built into GitHub
Workflows, events, jobs, steps, and actions: the hierarchy
YAML syntax basics for workflow files
Trigger events: push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch
Jobs and runners: ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest
Steps: running commands and using actions
Common CI use case: run tests on every pull request
Common CD use case: deploy to production on push to main
Secrets and environment variables: storing API keys securely
Matrix builds: testing across multiple versions
Workflow artifacts: uploading test results and build output
Debugging failed workflows: reading run logs
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're talking about GitHub Actions and workflows, which sounds technical, but for most contributors the practical question is much simpler: when GitHub runs automated checks on your pull request, what are those checks doing, what do the results mean, and what should you do next?

[JAMIE]
And that really matters in open source, because a person can make a perfectly good contribution and still feel stuck when a red X appears.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Automation is everywhere in real repositories. Tests run, linters run, docs builds run, accessibility scans run, and sometimes deployment previews run too. You do not need to become a workflow author to contribute well. But you do need to become comfortable reading the signals.

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the mechanics, I want to call out a few practical notes. This lesson has an audio companion role in the course, and it's also connected to earlier material on issue templates and related material on accessibility agents. And if you want the official reference for the platform itself, GitHub's documentation on understanding Actions is the authority.

[ALEX]
Well said. Also, if you're a blind or low-vision learner, this topic has a lot of interface reading in it, so we'll keep surfacing navigation strategies, not just definitions.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's start with the core idea. GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation system. A repository can define automated processes that run when certain events happen. For example, someone pushes commits, opens or updates a pull request, submits a review, posts a comment, or publishes a release.

[JAMIE]
So when people say, the checks are running, that's usually GitHub Actions behind the scenes?

[ALEX]
Often yes. Think of it as a configurable robot assistant for a repository. Maintainers tell that assistant what events to watch for and what jobs to run in response. Those jobs might test code, check formatting, scan for accessibility problems, check spelling, build documentation, or publish a preview version of a site.

[JAMIE]
And the key reassurance here is that contributors usually do not need to write the automation.

[ALEX]
Right. Most contributors are readers of workflow results, not authors of workflow files. Your everyday skill is understanding what ran, whether it passed, and what to fix if it did not.

[JAMIE]
Can we make that concrete for different learners?

[ALEX]
Yes. If you're using a screen reader, workflow files live in a folder named dot github, inside a subfolder named workflows. On GitHub, the T shortcut for go to file can help you search for files ending in dot yml there. The Actions tab sits in the repository navigation landmark, so in NVDA or JAWS you can jump by landmarks with D to find it quickly. And again, you do not need to write YAML just to contribute.

If you're a low-vision learner, it helps to know that the Actions tab uses a play-button style icon in the top navigation. Zooming in can make the label easier to catch. Workflow files use indentation-sensitive syntax, so in VS Code, larger font size and visible whitespace can make the structure much easier to read. On pull requests, the check results are paired with small colored icons, so zoom to a comfortable level and read the text beside the icons rather than relying on color alone.

And for sighted learners, the Actions tab is in the top repository navigation, and the quickest way to understand a workflow file is usually to open one in the Code tab and look for its trigger section and its job steps.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's build the vocabulary, because this topic gets confusing fast if all the words blur together.

[ALEX]
Good idea. A workflow is the complete automated process described in one YAML file. A repository can have many workflows.

A job is one major unit inside a workflow. Jobs usually run on their own machine environment.

A step is one task inside a job, like running a shell command or calling a reusable action.

An action is a reusable unit of automation, almost like a plugin. Many public actions are shared through GitHub Marketplace.

A runner is the machine that executes the job. Often it's a GitHub-hosted virtual server.

A trigger, or event, is what starts the workflow. Push, pull request, schedule, and manual launch are common examples.

A status check is the pass or fail result that appears on a pull request.

An artifact is a file produced by a workflow, like a report, build output, or downloadable package.

A secret is an encrypted value stored in repository settings so workflows can use sensitive data without exposing it directly.

And YAML is the format used to write workflow files. Indentation matters a lot.

[JAMIE]
There are also two little YAML keys that people see constantly: on and runs-on.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The key called on defines the trigger. The key called runs-on tells GitHub what operating system or runner environment to use, like ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, or macos-latest.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now where do these files actually live?

[ALEX]
In a very specific location: a folder named .github, and inside that, a folder named workflows. So the full path is .github slash workflows slash some-file-name dot yml.

[JAMIE]
And that location is not optional.

[ALEX]
Correct. GitHub expects workflow files there. Example names might include ci dot yml for tests, lint dot yml for style checks, a11y-scan dot yml for accessibility scanning, or deploy dot yml for deployment after merge.

[JAMIE]
That dot at the start of dot github matters too.

[ALEX]
It does. It means the folder is hidden by convention. On GitHub.com, you can still navigate to it in the file browser, or use the T shortcut to search for files. In VS Code, it appears in the Explorer, though some setups may require hidden files to be shown.

For screen reader users, it's useful to hear the folder name as dot github, then workflows inside it. And when you hear filenames ending in dot yml, those are workflow definitions written in YAML.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Can we walk through what a workflow file looks like without turning this into a YAML programming lesson?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Imagine a file named ci dot yml. At the top, it might say name: CI. That's the display name you'll often see in the Actions tab.

Then it has on, the trigger section. Maybe it runs on push to the main branch and also on pull_request targeting main.

Then it has jobs. Inside jobs, perhaps there is one job called test. That job says runs-on: ubuntu-latest, meaning it uses a Linux runner.

Then under steps, you might see a sequence like: check out the code, set up Node.js, install dependencies, and run tests.

[JAMIE]
So the logic is basically: when this event happens, run this job, and inside the job run these steps.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And reading a workflow file is usually easier if you ask three questions. First, what triggers it? Second, what jobs does it define? Third, what steps run inside those jobs?

[JAMIE]
And if the step that runs tests returns an error, the job fails, and that failure shows up on the pull request.

[ALEX]
That's the practical consequence. You do not need to memorize the syntax. You need to recognize the structure well enough to interpret what the automation is trying to do.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's talk triggers, because they explain why something ran when it did.

Common triggers include push, which means any commit pushed to a branch; pull_request, which covers a pull request being opened, updated, synchronized, or reopened; pull_request_review, when someone submits a review; issue_comment, when someone comments on an issue or PR; schedule, which is a recurring timer; workflow_dispatch, which allows a manual run from the Actions tab; release, when a release is published; and merge_group, which is used with merge queues.

[JAMIE]
If I'm contributing, the most important one is pull_request.

[ALEX]
Yes. That's usually what causes checks to appear on your PR. Sometimes push also matters, especially if the repository runs checks on every branch update, but pull_request is the one most contributors experience directly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay, now the part learners really care about: the status checks on a pull request.

[ALEX]
When you open a PR in a repository that uses GitHub Actions, you'll usually find a checks or status checks section on the Conversation tab, often near the merge area.

A spinning yellow or orange indicator means checks are still running. Wait.

A green checkmark means the relevant checks passed.

A red X means one or more checks failed, and you should read the failure before trying to merge.

A gray slashed circle usually means a check was skipped, often intentionally.

And sometimes you'll encounter a warning state that is not a hard blocker. It still deserves review, but it may not prevent merging.

[JAMIE]
That distinction matters, because learners often see anything that's not green and assume disaster.

[ALEX]
Right. Not every non-green state means you broke the project.

[JAMIE]
What about navigating this with a screen reader?

[ALEX]
For NVDA or JAWS in browse mode, open the pull request Conversation tab, jump by headings with H or by heading level if that works well in your setup, find the checks section, then move through the individual check items. Each result is typically announced as a link or button with its name and status. Activate a failed check with Enter to reveal or open more detail.

For VoiceOver on macOS in Safari, open the Rotor with VO+U, move to Headings, locate the checks section, then read through the listed results with VO navigation. Activate a selected check with VO+Space.

[JAMIE]
And then there's the idea of required versus non-required checks.

[ALEX]
Yes. Required checks must pass before a PR can be merged. Non-required checks are informative. They may still point to a real problem, but they are not configured as merge blockers.

[JAMIE]
So if I see a failed non-required check, I shouldn't ignore it automatically, but I also shouldn't assume the merge button is permanently blocked.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The right question is, is this required, and what is it telling me? A useful mental model here is: status checks are automated reviewers. They do not replace human review, but they often catch predictable problems quickly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's move to the Actions tab itself, because sometimes the pull request only shows the summary and you need to inspect the run.

[ALEX]
That's right. The Actions tab is where you can browse workflow runs across the repository. On GitHub, it's in the repository's main navigation.

For screen reader users, a reliable way to reach it is to jump through landmarks or tab through the repository navigation until you hear Actions. Once there, you'll find a list of workflow runs, often with the workflow name, branch, triggering event, commit message, time, and status.

[JAMIE]
How would someone navigate that list efficiently in NVDA or JAWS?

[ALEX]
In browse mode, use heading navigation and links navigation to move among workflow names and run entries. The page is often structured with headings, links, and status text. Open the run you want, then explore the jobs and steps. If the page feels busy, switching between browse mode reading and focused interaction can help.

[JAMIE]
And in VoiceOver on macOS?

[ALEX]
Use the Rotor to jump among headings, links, and landmarks. Once inside a run page, VO navigation can move through job names and step entries. The key is to identify the status summary first, then the failing job, then the failing step.

[JAMIE]
What details should a learner expect inside one run?

[ALEX]
Usually you'll find the overall result, then one or more jobs, and within each job a sequence of steps. Expanding a failed step reveals log output. That log is often the most important evidence: it tells you what command ran and what error it produced.

Sometimes the run also includes artifacts, such as generated reports or preview outputs, which can be downloaded.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now let's name the kinds of workflows learners are likely to encounter over and over.

[ALEX]
First, continuous integration, or CI. This is the general category for automatically building and testing the project whenever code changes.

Second, linting or code style checks. These look for formatting problems, style violations, or patterns the project considers incorrect.

Third, spelling and documentation checks. These catch typos, broken docs builds, malformed markdown, or documentation rules.

Fourth, accessibility scanning. These workflows try to detect common accessibility issues, often in web content.

Fifth, security scanning. These look for known vulnerable dependencies, insecure patterns, or other security concerns.

Sixth, deployment or preview builds. These create a temporary preview of a site or publish a new version after changes are merged.

[JAMIE]
I like that list because it helps learners interpret a check name. If the workflow is called CI, it probably runs tests. If it's called lint, it's probably style. If it's called preview, it may be building something you can inspect.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The workflow name is a clue about the kind of feedback you're getting.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's tackle the emotional side and the practical side together: what should you do when a check fails?

[ALEX]
Step one: don't panic. A failed check is information, not a judgment about your worth or your ability.

Step two: navigate to the failed check. From the PR checks section or the Actions tab, open the failed run.

Step three: find the failing step. Don't stop at the workflow name. You need the exact job and exact step that failed.

Step four: read the error message carefully. Look for the command that ran, the file involved, the line number if one is given, and whether the issue is a test failure, formatting issue, missing dependency, syntax error, or something else.

Step five: fix the issue locally or in the web editor, depending on the kind of change and the repository's workflow. Some problems are quick text edits. Others are best fixed in VS Code where you can run tools locally.

Step six: commit and push the fix. That usually retriggers the relevant checks automatically.

Step seven: if you're stuck, ask for help. Leave a comment on the PR or issue, explain what check failed, what you already tried, and what part you don't understand.

[JAMIE]
Let's slow that down with a realistic example. Suppose the lint check fails.

[ALEX]
Then the failing step might say something like run linter, and the log may point to a file with a formatting problem. Maybe a line is too long, indentation is off, or a style rule was violated. You fix the file, commit, push, and the lint workflow runs again.

[JAMIE]
And if the CI test fails?

[ALEX]
The log may show a test name, expected versus actual output, or a missing setup step. In a beginner-friendly repository, this may still be something you can fix. In a more complex project, you may need maintainer guidance. The important skill is locating and naming the failure clearly.

[JAMIE]
So a useful learning card here would be: failed check, open it; failing workflow is not enough, find the failing step; read the message; make a fix; push again; ask for help if needed.

[ALEX]
Perfect summary.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now security and permissions. This is the part where learners can accidentally click through prompts without understanding the risk.

[ALEX]
Yes, and that is worth taking seriously. Some workflows need approval before they can run, especially in contexts involving pull requests from forks or contributors who do not yet have trusted status in the repository. The reason is security. Workflows can execute code, and maintainers need to protect secrets, infrastructure, and deployment systems.

[JAMIE]
So if a workflow says it is waiting for approval, that is not a personal rejection.

[ALEX]
Not at all. It's a guardrail.

[JAMIE]
What should contributors never do?

[ALEX]
Never paste secrets, tokens, passwords, API keys, or private credentials into workflow files, issue comments, pull request comments, logs, or screenshots. Never approve or modify automation you do not understand just because you're trying to make a red message disappear. And never assume that because something is automated, it is automatically safe.

[JAMIE]
What about Dependabot?

[ALEX]
Dependabot is GitHub's tool for automated dependency updates and some security-related pull requests. You may see PRs created by it, and repositories may have workflows that respond to those updates. The key contributor takeaway is that automated dependency PRs are normal, but they are still subject to checks, review, and security awareness.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's spend real time on accessibility-focused workflows, since this course cares about accessible contribution practices.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Some repositories run accessibility-specific workflows. GitHub has its own accessibility-related scanning action offerings, and many projects use other common tools in a11y workflows as well.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of tools are we talking about?

[ALEX]
Often browser-based or static analysis tools that catch issues like missing alt text, insufficient form labels, color contrast concerns detectable from code, missing ARIA attributes in certain contexts, heading structure problems, or landmark-related issues. Commonly used tooling in the broader ecosystem includes automated accessibility checkers integrated into CI pipelines.

[JAMIE]
But we should be careful not to oversell them.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Automated tools catch some problems, not all problems. They are very good at repeatable rule-based checks. They are not good at judging whether alt text is meaningful, whether focus order makes sense in a complex interaction, whether instructions are understandable, or whether the overall user experience works well with assistive technology.

[JAMIE]
So if an accessibility workflow passes, that does not prove the experience is fully accessible.

[ALEX]
Correct. It means the automated checks did not detect certain known issues. That's useful, but incomplete.

[JAMIE]
The source also mentions preparing the environment for GitHub-hosted agents.

[ALEX]
Yes. In accessibility workflows, the runner often needs the right environment before scans can succeed. That may include installing dependencies, setting up a browser, building the site, launching a local server, or ensuring the app is reachable to the scanning tool. In other words, accessibility scanning in Actions usually depends on ordinary setup steps being correct first.

[JAMIE]
So a failed a11y scan may actually mean the site never built or the test environment never started.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Always read the failing step before assuming the accessibility findings themselves are the problem.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's make this hands-on. If a learner wants to explore a workflow in a repository, what should they do?

[ALEX]
Here's a good activity. Go to the repository's Code area and look for the .github slash workflows folder. Open a workflow file, perhaps ci dot yml or something similarly named.

Then identify these pieces: the workflow name, the trigger or triggers under on, the jobs that are defined, the runner listed under runs-on, and the steps inside a job.

Next, visit the Actions tab and locate a recent run of that workflow. Open it and answer a few questions for yourself: what event triggered this run, did it pass or fail, which job ran, and what steps were included?

If there is a failed run available, try to find the exact failing step and read its log message.

[JAMIE]
And if this is being used as a class or self-study discussion?

[ALEX]
Good discussion questions include: what is this workflow trying to protect or verify? Which trigger matters most for contributors? If it failed, would the likely fix be in code, documentation, configuration, or infrastructure? And how easy was it to navigate the run details with your current accessibility tools?

[JAMIE]
I really like that last one, because it treats accessibility as part of the workflow experience, not as an afterthought.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
We should also be honest about what we're not covering.

[ALEX]
Yes. We are not teaching full workflow authoring, advanced YAML design, matrix builds, custom composite actions, caching strategies, reusable workflows, self-hosted runners, deployment architecture, or deep GitHub Actions security engineering. Those are real topics, just beyond the scope of a contributor-focused introduction.

[JAMIE]
So where should learners go next?

[ALEX]
Start with GitHub Docs for workflow syntax and understanding Actions. Check GitHub's changelog for evolving features. Review GitHub's security guidance for secure use and hardening of Actions. And if your goal is contribution rather than automation engineering, stay grounded in the basics we've covered today: know where workflows live, know what triggers them, know how to read checks, and know how to respond when something fails.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's wrap it up. GitHub Actions is the automation system many repositories use to run tests, checks, scans, and builds. Workflows live in .github slash workflows and are written in YAML. They are triggered by events like push or pull request. On your PR, their results appear as status checks.

[JAMIE]
Your job as a contributor is usually not to write the automation. It's to interpret it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Learn the vocabulary: workflow, job, step, action, runner, trigger, status check, artifact, secret. Learn the common statuses: running, passed, failed, skipped, warning. Learn how to navigate the checks section and the Actions tab with your screen reader or visual setup. And when a check fails, don't panic. Open the run, find the failing step, read the error, fix what you can, push again, and ask for help when needed.

[JAMIE]
And for accessibility work especially, remember that automated a11y checks are useful but partial. They support human judgment; they do not replace it.

[ALEX]
Well said. The more comfortable you become reading automation, the more confident you'll feel contributing to real projects.

[JAMIE]
And the next time a red X appears, you'll know it's not the end of the story. It's the start of an investigation.

# Appendix Q: GitHub Actions and Workflows
>
> **Listen to Episode 34:** [GitHub Actions and Workflows](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 17: Issue Templates](17-issue-templates.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 19](19-accessibility-agents.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: Understanding Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/learn-github-actions/understanding-github-actions)

## Understanding Automation in Open Source Repositories

> **Why this matters for you:** Every time you open a pull request on a real open source project, automated processes will run. Understanding what they are, what they mean, and what to do when they fail is essential to being a confident contributor.

## Table of Contents

1. [What Is GitHub Actions?](#1-what-is-github-actions)
2. [Key Vocabulary](#2-key-vocabulary)
3. [Where Workflows Live in a Repository](#3-where-workflows-live-in-a-repository)
4. [The Anatomy of a Workflow File](#4-the-anatomy-of-a-workflow-file)
5. [What Triggers a Workflow](#5-what-triggers-a-workflow)
6. [Understanding Status Checks on Pull Requests](#6-understanding-status-checks-on-pull-requests)
7. [Reading the Actions Tab with a Screen Reader](#7-reading-the-actions-tab-with-a-screen-reader)
8. [Common Workflows You Will Encounter](#8-common-workflows-you-will-encounter)
9. [What To Do When a Check Fails](#9-what-to-do-when-a-check-fails)
10. [Workflow Permissions and Security](#10-workflow-permissions-and-security)
11. [Accessibility-Focused Workflows](#11-accessibility-focused-workflows)
12. [Hands-On Activity](#12-hands-on-activity)
13. [What We Are NOT Covering (And Where to Learn More)](#13-what-we-are-not-covering-and-where-to-learn-more)

## 1. What Is GitHub Actions?

**GitHub Actions** is GitHub's built-in automation system. It lets repository maintainers define automated tasks that run in response to things that happen in the repository - like someone opening a pull request, pushing a commit, or filing an issue.

Think of it as a robot assistant that every repository can optionally configure. That robot watches for specific events and then automatically runs jobs: testing code, checking spelling, scanning for accessibility issues, building documentation, deploying a website, and more.

**As a contributor, you do not need to write workflows.** But you will see their results on nearly every pull request you open, and you need to understand what those results mean.

### Learning Cards: What Is GitHub Actions

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Workflow files live in `.github/workflows/` — use T (Go to file) on any repo page to search for `.yml` files in that directory
- The Actions tab is in the repository navigation landmark — press D (NVDA/JAWS) to jump between landmarks and find it
- You do not need to write YAML to contribute — your job is to read the status check results on your PR and fix any issues they flag

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The Actions tab icon (a play-button triangle) sits in the repo's top navigation bar — zoom in if the icon-only display is hard to read; the word "Actions" appears next to it
- Workflow YAML files use indentation-sensitive syntax — increase your editor font size and enable visible whitespace to distinguish nesting levels
- Status check results on your PR use small colored icons (green checkmark, red X, yellow spinner) — zoom to 150%+ to read the text labels beside them

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Find the Actions tab in the repository's top navigation bar between Projects and Security — a play-button icon marks it
- Workflow files are YAML files in `.github/workflows/` — open any one in the Code tab to see the triggers (`on:`) and job steps
- On your PR, scroll to the checks section near the merge box to see green checkmarks (passed), red X marks (failed), or yellow spinners (running)

</details>

## 2. Key Vocabulary

| Term | What It Means |
| ------  | ---------------  |
| **Workflow** | A complete automated process defined in a YAML file. A repo can have many workflows. |
| **Job** | A group of steps that run together, usually on the same machine. A workflow can have multiple jobs. |
| **Step** | A single task within a job - running a command, calling an action, etc. |
| **Action** | A reusable unit of automation. Like a plugin. Many are shared publicly on [GitHub Marketplace](https://github.com/marketplace?type=actions). |
| **Runner** | The machine (virtual server) that executes a job. GitHub provides free runners. |
| **Trigger / Event** | The thing that causes a workflow to start - a push, a PR, a schedule, etc. |
| **Status check** | The pass/fail result of a workflow shown on a pull request. |
| **Artifact** | A file produced by a workflow (a build output, a test report, etc.) that can be downloaded. |
| **Secret** | An encrypted variable stored in a repo's settings - used in workflows without exposing sensitive values. |
| **YAML** | The file format used to write workflow files. Indentation matters. |
| **`on:`** | The YAML key that defines what triggers a workflow. |
| **`runs-on:`** | The YAML key that specifies the runner OS (`ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest`, `macos-latest`). |

## 3. Where Workflows Live in a Repository

Workflow files live in a specific, mandatory location:

### Description

Workflow files live at your-repository/.github/workflows/. Example files include: ci.yml (runs tests on every push or PR), lint.yml (checks code style), a11y-scan.yml (accessibility scanning), and deploy.yml (deploys the site when code merges to main).

The `.github/` folder is hidden by convention (starts with a dot). To find it:

- **On GitHub.com:** The file browser shows it - use `T` (go to file) or navigate the file table with `Ctrl+Alt+Arrow` keys
- **In VS Code:** It appears in the Explorer panel - enable "Show Hidden Files" if needed

> **Screen reader tip:** The `.github` folder reads as "dot github." The `workflows` folder is inside it. File names ending in `.yml` are YAML workflow files.

## 4. The Anatomy of a Workflow File

Here is a simple, real workflow file. You do not need to write this, but you should be able to read it:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml

name: CI                          # The display name shown in the Actions tab

on:                               # What triggers this workflow
  push:
    branches: [main]              # Run when code is pushed to main
  pull_request:                   # Run when a PR is opened or updated
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:                           # The job name (shown in status checks)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest        # What operating system to use
    steps:
      - name: Check out code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4 # A reusable action - downloads your repo code

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install          # A shell command

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test             # Another shell command
```

**Reading this:** The workflow named "CI" runs when code is pushed to `main` or a PR targets `main`. It creates one job called `test` that runs on Linux. That job checks out the code, installs Node.js, installs dependencies, and runs the test suite.

If `npm test` exits with an error, the job fails, and that failure shows up as a red on your pull request.

## 5. What Triggers a Workflow

The most common triggers you will encounter as a contributor:

| Trigger | What Causes It |
| ---------  | ---------------  |
| `push` | Any commit pushed to a branch |
| `pull_request` | A PR is opened, updated, synchronized, or reopened |
| `pull_request_review` | A review is submitted on a PR |
| `issue_comment` | A comment is posted on an issue or PR |
| `schedule` | A recurring timer (like a cron job) - e.g., every Monday at 9am |
| `workflow_dispatch` | A manual trigger - someone activates a button in the Actions tab |
| `release` | When a new release is published |
| `merge_group` | When a PR enters a merge queue |

**The most important one for you:** `pull_request` - this is what triggers checks on your PR.

## 6. Understanding Status Checks on Pull Requests

When you open a pull request on a repo that uses GitHub Actions, you will see a section near the bottom of the **Conversation tab** called **checks** or **status checks**.

### What the status indicators mean

| Symbol | Color | Meaning | What to do |
| --------  | -------  | ---------  | -----------  |
| Spinning circle | Yellow/Orange | Checks are running - wait | Wait for them to complete |
| Checkmark | Green | All required checks passed | Good - you may be able to merge |
| X (cross) | Red | One or more checks failed | Do not merge - read the failure |
| Slashed circle | Grey | Check was skipped | Usually fine - skipped by design |
| | Yellow | Non-blocking warning | Review but may not block merge |

### Navigating status checks with a screen reader

#### NVDA / JAWS (browse mode)

1. Open the pull request Conversation tab
2. Navigate to the section heading for "checks" using `H` or `2`
3. Each check result is announced as a link or button with its name and status
4. Press `Enter` on a failed check to expand its details

#### VoiceOver (macOS, Safari)

1. Use `VO+U` to open the Rotor
2. Select "Headings" and navigate to the checks section
3. Use `VO+Arrow` to read through check results
4. Activate a check link with `VO+Space`

### Required vs. non-required checks

- **Required checks** must pass before a PR can be merged. A maintainer configures which checks are required in Branch Protection Rules.
- **Non-required checks** are informational - a failure shown in grey/yellow usually won't block a merge.
- If you're not sure whether a check is required, look for the phrase **"Required"** next to the check name.

## 7. Reading the Actions Tab with a Screen Reader

The **Actions tab** of a repository shows the history of all workflow runs. You can use it to see what ran, what failed, and why.

### Getting to the Actions tab

1. Open the repository
2. Navigate to the "Repository navigation" landmark (`D` on NVDA/JAWS)
3. Find the "Actions" tab link and activate it (`Enter`)

### Navigating workflow runs (NVDA/JAWS browse mode)

```text
Key          Action
H            Jump between section headings
3            Jump between workflow run headings (they are h3)
Tab          Move between interactive elements (links, buttons)
Enter        Open a workflow run to see details
```

### Navigating workflow runs (VoiceOver macOS)

```text
Key                  Action
VO+U → Headings      Open rotor and navigate by heading
VO+Right/Left        Read next/previous item
VO+Space             Activate a link or button
```

### Reading a run's details

When you open a workflow run, you see:

- Job names listed on the left (or in a sidebar)
- Steps listed within each job
- Green checkmarks (passed) or red X marks (failed) next to each step

To find out **why a step failed:**

1. Navigate to the failed step
2. Activate it to expand the log output
3. The log is a large text area - switch to focus mode to read it
4. Look for lines containing `Error:`, `FAILED`, `exit code`, or `AssertionError`

> **Tip:** Log output can be very long. Use your screen reader's search (`NVDA+Ctrl+F`, `JAWS: Insert+F`, `VO+F`) to search for "error" or "failed" to jump directly to the problem.

## 8. Common Workflows You Will Encounter

As you contribute to open source repositories, you will see these types of workflows regularly:

### Continuous Integration (CI)

**What it does:** Runs the project's test suite automatically every time code changes.

**What you see:** A check called "CI", "Tests", "Build", or similar.

**If it fails:** Your code change may have broken one or more tests. Read the error message in the job log, or ask the maintainer if it is a pre-existing failure.

### Linting / Code Style

**What it does:** Checks that code follows the project's formatting and style rules - things like indentation, line length, or consistent import ordering.

**What you see:** A check called "Lint", "ESLint", "Prettier", "Flake8", or similar.

**If it fails:** Usually means a formatting rule was violated. The log will tell you exactly which file and line. Many projects include a command to auto-fix this (e.g., `npm run lint:fix`).

### Spelling / Documentation Checks

**What it does:** Checks documentation files for spelling errors, broken links, or formatting issues.

**What you see:** A check called "Spell Check", "markdownlint", "Link Check", or similar.

**If it fails:** There is a typo or formatting issue in a doc file. Very common on documentation-only contributions.

### Accessibility Scanning

**What it does:** Runs automated accessibility checks against HTML output or component libraries to catch WCAG violations.

**What you see:** A check called "a11y", "Accessibility", "axe", "pa11y", or similar.

**If it fails:** An accessibility problem was introduced. The log will describe the failing rule (e.g., "Image missing alt text", "Color contrast insufficient"). This is extremely valuable information and exactly the kind of thing this community cares about.

### Security Scanning

**What it does:** Scans for known vulnerabilities in dependencies or exposed secrets.

**What you see:** A check called "CodeQL", "Dependabot", "Snyk", or similar.

**If it fails:** A security issue was detected - inform the maintainer and do not merge.

### Deployment / Preview Builds

**What it does:** Builds and deploys a preview version of a website or app from your PR branch.

**What you see:** A bot comment on your PR with a preview URL, and a check called "Deploy", "Netlify", "Vercel", "GitHub Pages", or similar.

**What it gives you:** A live preview of what the site will look like with your changes - very useful for visual review and for accessibility testing with your screen reader on the actual rendered output.

## 9. What To Do When a Check Fails

This happens to every contributor. It is normal. Here is your step-by-step process:

### Step 1: Don't panic

A failing check is information, not a judgment. It is the system telling you something specific needs attention.

### Step 2: Navigate to the failed check

From your PR's Conversation tab:

1. Scroll down to the checks section (press `D` to reach the "Checks" region if using a screen reader)
2. Find the failing check (red X)
3. Press `Enter` on "Details" (or the check name itself) to open the workflow run

### Step 3: Find the failing step

In the workflow run:

1. Look for the step with the red X marker
2. Press `Enter` or `Space` to expand the log output

### Step 4: Read the error message

Look for:

- `Error:` - describes what went wrong
- `FAILED` or `FAIL` - test failure summary
- File name and line number - where exactly the problem is
- `exit code 1` (or non-zero) - the command failed

### Step 5: Fix the issue locally (or in the web editor)

Common fixes:

- **Test failure:** Understand what the test expects and whether your change broke something intentional
- **Lint failure:** Run the project's format/lint command, or manually fix the flagged lines
- **Spell check failure:** Fix the typo noted in the log
- **Accessibility failure:** Fix the specific a11y violation described (missing alt text, contrast issue, etc.)

### Step 6: Commit and push the fix

- The workflow will automatically re-run when you push new commits to the branch
- No need to close and re-open the PR

### Step 7: If you're stuck

It is completely acceptable to comment on your PR:

> "The CI check is failing on [step name]. I've read the error log and I'm not sure how to fix [specific issue]. Could a maintainer point me in the right direction?"

Asking for help is not weakness. It is collaboration.

### Learning Cards: What To Do When a Check Fails

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- From the failing check's Details link, the log page has a sidebar listing job steps — the failed step has focus or is announced as "failed"; expand it to read the error
- Use your screen reader's find command (NVDA+Ctrl+F, JAWS: Insert+F) to search the log for "Error:" or "FAILED" — this skips hundreds of passing log lines
- After pushing a fix, return to the PR page — checks re-run automatically and the status updates from red X to yellow spinner to green checkmark

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- CI log pages can be very long with small monospace text — use Ctrl+F in your browser to search for "Error" or "FAIL" rather than scrolling through everything
- The failing step is marked with a red X icon in the left sidebar of the log page — zoom in to identify it, then click to expand only that step
- If you cannot read the log comfortably, copy the error text and paste it into your editor at a larger font size

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- On the workflow run page, the left sidebar shows all job steps — the failing step has a red X icon; click it to jump directly to the error output
- Error messages are usually highlighted in red within the log output — scan for red text and the phrases "Error:", "FAILED", or "exit code 1"
- After pushing a fix, watch for the yellow spinner on the PR page to confirm that checks are re-running

</details>

## 10. Workflow Permissions and Security

### Why some workflows need your approval

If you are contributing to a repository for the first time, GitHub may hold your workflow runs for approval. You will see a message like:

> "Workflows aren't being run on this pull request. A maintainer must approve this."

This is a **security feature** - it prevents malicious code from running on the maintainer's infrastructure before they have reviewed it. Do not be alarmed. Simply add a comment like:

> "Ready for review. Could a maintainer approve the workflow runs?"

### What you should never do

- Never change workflow files to bypass checks (e.g., deleting tests to make them pass)
- Never add secrets or credentials to workflow files or code
- Never approve a workflow run on someone else's PR unless you have reviewed the code

### Dependabot

**Dependabot** is an automated bot built into GitHub that creates pull requests to update outdated or vulnerable dependencies. You will see PRs in a repository from a user called `dependabot[bot]`. These are automated, not from a person. Maintainers typically review and merge these. As a contributor, you usually don't need to interact with them, but it is good to know they exist.

## 11. Accessibility-Focused Workflows

This is relevant to our event specifically. The open source accessibility community actively uses GitHub Actions to **automatically catch accessibility regressions** - meaning, to ensure that new code does not introduce new accessibility barriers.

### GitHub's Accessibility Scanner Action

GitHub itself has open-sourced an [AI-powered Accessibility Scanner](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/accessibility-scanner) that can be added to a repository. It uses AI to find, file, and help fix accessibility bugs using GitHub Copilot.

A basic workflow using it looks like this:

```yaml
name: Accessibility Scan

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  a11y:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run Accessibility Scanner
        uses: github/accessibility-scanner@v1
        with:
          github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

### Common tools used in a11y workflows

| Tool | What It Checks |
| ------  | ----------------  |
| [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core) | WCAG violations in HTML/rendered pages |
| [pa11y](https://pa11y.org/) | Automated accessibility testing against URLs |
| [jest-axe](https://github.com/nickcolley/jest-axe) | axe checks inside unit tests |
| [Lighthouse CI](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/lighthouse-ci) | Accessibility + performance scoring |
| [IBM Equal Access Checker](https://github.com/IBMa/equal-access) | WCAG 2.1 / 2.2 compliance checking |

#### What these tools catch (and what they do not)

Automated tools catch approximately **30-40% of accessibility issues** - things like missing alt attributes, insufficient color contrast ratios, or unlabeled form fields. The remaining issues require human testing, especially with actual assistive technology like your screen reader.

This is precisely why **manual testing by people who use screen readers is so valuable and irreplaceable.**

### Preparing the Environment for GitHub-Hosted Agents

When custom agents run on GitHub.com - triggered by an issue assignment or a Copilot Chat task - they need any external tools pre-installed before they start working. GitHub recognizes a special setup workflow for this: a workflow file with a single job named `copilot-setup-steps`.

**Location:** `.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml`

```yaml
name: Copilot Setup Steps

on: workflow_dispatch

jobs:
  copilot-setup-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install accessibility testing tools
        run: npm install -g @axe-core/cli markdownlint-cli2
```

**What this does:** Before a Copilot coding agent begins working, GitHub runs this job to prepare the environment. Without it, an agent that needs `markdownlint-cli2` (for the Markdown Accessibility Assistant) or `@axe-core/cli` (for WCAG scanning) will fail because those tools are not present.

**The job name `copilot-setup-steps` is required** - GitHub won't recognize any other name for agent environment preparation.

**Connection to Section 13 of the VS Code guide:** This is the infrastructure that enables Scope 3 (cloud execution) of the three-layer Accessibility Agents model. The same agent you run in VS Code with `@markdown-accessibility-assistant` can run on GitHub.com automatically - but only if the environment is prepared with this workflow.

| Triggers fire workflows | `push`, `pull_request`, `schedule` are the most common |
| Status checks appear on your PR | Green checkmark, Red X, Yellow circle = pass, fail, running |

| a11y workflows catch ~30-40% of issues | Human screen reader testing catches the rest |

> ### Day 2 Bridge - From Actions to Agentic Workflows
>
> **Understand standard YAML workflow files before engaging with agentic workflows.** GitHub Agentic Workflows are not a separate technology - they are the next layer on top of what you learned here. They share the same trigger model, the same permissions system, and the same `.github/workflows/` directory. You cannot evaluate whether an agentic workflow is safe or correct unless you can already read a standard one.
>
> The three layers, in sequence - each builds on the one before it:
>
> 1. **Standard GitHub Actions** - YAML files in `.github/workflows/`; define triggers and structured shell steps; what you mastered in this guide
> 2. **Accessibility Agents in VS Code** - `.agent.md` files in `.github/agents/`; define behavior in plain English; GitHub Copilot Chat executes them on demand in your editor - same `.github/` folder, plain text, no YAML required
> 3. **GitHub Agentic Workflows in the cloud** - `.md` files in `.github/workflows/`; define intent in plain Markdown frontmatter; a coding agent (Copilot CLI, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex) executes them inside GitHub Actions on any trigger - no VS Code, no local setup required
>
> All three live in `.github/`. All three are plain text. All three run on your behalf. The only difference is where they run and how sophisticated their executor is.
>
> *You cannot skip a layer. Each one only makes sense because you understand the one before it.*

Completing Challenge 15 unlocks Challenge 16 (Capstone Project) plus Bonus Challenges A through E. The bonus challenges are a structured unlock path, not "things to do if you finish early".

Challenge 16 is titled "Capstone Project". It accepts contributions to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or any other meaningful repository. Review-ready drafts and contribution plans are valid evidence of completion.
The Learning Room repository is where Day 1 contributions happen (issue, branch, commit, pull request, merge). It is provisioned per learner.
Hosts are Alex (warm expert) and Jamie (curious co-host who asks the questions learners hesitate to ask). They are colleagues, not teacher and student.
voiceRules.voiceExemplar:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[JAMIE]
I like that. You've already used a professional issue template, so now you reverse-engineer it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Also, there's an administrative note here: this chapter is meant to prepare you for a later workflow using a template-building agent. The advice is to complete the manual template chapter first, then use the automation later.

[JAMIE]
And time-wise?

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.

[JAMIE]
That feels approachable. First understand an existing template, then adapt one, then optionally build another version from scratch, then verify it works.

[ALEX]
That's the idea. The workshop recommendation frames Challenge 14 as design-focused rather than automation-focused. You're producing evidence of understanding, often as an issue comment or a pull request, rather than trying to satisfy a complicated code runtime.

[JAMIE]
Though there is still one small autograded requirement in the challenge template itself.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the assigned challenge issue, the autograder checks that a YAML file exists in the repository
